dataset.what_one_row_represents: The largest file (expected_points_df.csv) has one row per league fixture in Europe's big-five leagues. The manager-tenure files have one row per manager-club tenure. The team-season file has one row per team-season pair.
dataset.geographic_scope: Europe's big-five leagues: England, Spain, Germany, Italy, France

ana_01.label: Coverage: 5 leagues, 15 seasons, 27,390 fixtures
ana_01.content: The dataset covers 27,390 individual league fixtures from Europe's big-five leagues — England, Spain, Italy, France, and Germany — across 15 seasons from August 2004 through May 2019. Forecast model errors averaged 7.27 points per team-season (median 5.99); the league-by-league mean absolute error ranges from a tight 7.01 in France to 7.50 in England. The Pearson correlation between expected and actual points-per-game across all 1,470 team-seasons is 0.796, confirming the FIFA-rating-based forecast tracks reality closely.

calculation.output:

Mean absolute error per season: 7.27 points
Median absolute error per season: 5.99
By league: England=7.50, France=7.01, Germany=7.37, Italy=7.45, Spain=7.05
Pearson r (expected vs actual): 0.796

ana_02.label: Manager population: 598 distinct managers, 1,220 tenures
ana_02.content: The data includes 1,220 manager-tenure rows across 598 distinct managers and 192 distinct clubs. Of these, 502 tenures lasted at least one full season (38+ league games). The currently-employed manager-board at end-2018 contained 596 names — most of whom appear in the data with only a single, short tenure.

Distinct managers: 598
Distinct teams: 192
Currently-employed managers (manager_ratings_df): 596

ana_03.label: The headline distribution: most managers cluster around zero
ana_03.content: Across 502 manager-tenures of at least one full season, the average manager added 0.04 points per game above what FIFA-based player ratings predicted — a margin so close to zero it is statistically indistinguishable from luck for any single tenure. The standard deviation is 0.18 points-per-game; the 5th-95th percentile range runs only from -0.24 to +0.34. About 45% of all tenures fall within ±0.10 ppg of expectation. Just 16% of managers cleared +0.20 ppg over a full-season-or-more sample, and only a handful exceeded +0.40. This is the spine of the story: the typical manager is a rounding error.

ana_04.label: The exceptions: top 12 over-performing tenures
ana_04.content: The top of the leaderboard is dominated by single-season improbabilities rather than household names. Abelardo's 42-game stint at Deportivo Alavés tops the list at +0.57 points-per-game above expectation; Ralph Hasenhüttl's RB Leipzig tenure (+0.55) and Luciano Spalletti's two stretches at Udinese (+0.54) and Roma (+0.52) follow. Claudio Ranieri's miracle Leicester title campaign appears mid-table at +0.47 — a reminder that even the most famous over-achievement of the decade was, on this metric, of similar magnitude to a dozen lesser-known runs. Below the very top, the curve flattens fast: by tenure 12 you are at +0.41, only 0.05 ppg below the leader.

ana_05.label: The active board: top 10 currently-employed managers
ana_05.content: After applying the regression-to-the-mean shrinkage that best predicts future results, the top 10 active managers in late 2018 cluster within a 1.2-point range of each other. Lucien Favre tops the list at +3.76 projected points added per season above an average coach with the same squad, followed by Rudi Garcia (+3.40), Diego Simeone (+3.27), and Maurizio Sarri (+3.04). Jürgen Klopp lands sixth at +2.85 — backed by 466 prior career matches that anchor the projection. Every name in the top 10 has built their reputation on at least 100 prior career matches, and most on more than 250.

ana_07.label: Most active managers project as below-average
ana_07.content: Of the 596 currently-employed-or-recently-employed managers in the database, 432 (72.5%) have a negative projection — meaning the model expects them to win fewer points per season than a hypothetical league-average coach with the same squad. Just 44 managers (7.4%) project as adding more than one point per season; 74 (12.4%) clear half a point. Half the population sits within ±0.5 points-per-season of league-average, which over a 38-game campaign is one decisive corner kick away from indistinguishable. The mean projection is -0.25, the median -0.36 — a heavily left-skewed distribution where most coaches do not earn their wage.

ana_08.label: The killer test: past overperformance barely predicts future
ana_08.content: Among 222 managers with at least two distinct tenures, the correlation between first-tenure and second-tenure points-per-game above expectation is just r = 0.04 (p = 0.54) — statistically indistinguishable from no relationship at all. The conditional probability that a manager who overperformed in tenure one will overperform again in tenure two is only 45%, barely better than the 36.6% rate observed for managers who underperformed in tenure one. The data refuses to grant managers a stable 'level of skill' that travels with them.

ana_09.label: Quartile collapse: every group of managers regresses to roughly zero
ana_09.content: Split the 222 multi-tenure managers into quartiles by their first-tenure points-per-game above expectation, then look at how the same managers performed in their next tenure. Every quartile, including the very top one, collapses back toward zero. The bottom-quartile managers (who started at a mean of about -0.4 ppg below expectation) ended their second tenure at -0.04 ppg; the top-quartile managers (who started at about +0.3) ended at -0.001. The pattern is regression to the mean in its purest visible form: the apparent 'good' and 'bad' coaches of round one converge in round two.

data_table.description: Mean tenure-2 ppg-above-expectation, grouped by tenure-1 quartile

ana_15.label: Sir Alex Ferguson: the canonical outlier
ana_15.content: Across his 342 league games at Manchester United covered by this dataset (1986-2013, restricted to data-available seasons), Sir Alex Ferguson averaged 2.25 points per game versus an expected 2.09 — a margin of +0.159 ppg above expectation. Over a 38-game season that is roughly six extra league points; over a quarter-century career it accumulates relentlessly. Ferguson's tenure of 342 games and steady positive margin is exactly the kind of profile the shrinkage formula rewards: even with 461 games of zero performance added, his record retains roughly 43% of its weight.

ana_16.label: Klopp's three-club arc: the textbook over-performer
ana_16.content: Jürgen Klopp's career across three clubs reads like a textbook over-performance trajectory. At Mainz (2001-08, 102 games covered) he edged 0.05 ppg above expectation. At Borussia Dortmund (2008-15, 238 games) he leapt to +0.17 ppg — the spine of the original Economist piece's third chart. At Liverpool (from October 2015, 126 games covered) he rose again to +0.31 ppg. The line goes only one way, and crucially each step is built on enough games (>100) to make luck-based explanations implausible.

data_table.description: Klopp's three tenures: actual vs expected ppg

ana_17.label: Famous-name tenure profiles for comparison
ana_17.content: A grid of well-known managers shows how varied their measured impact actually is. Pep Guardiola's three clubs all post positive margins, but only modestly: +0.11 at Barcelona, +0.08 at Bayern, +0.28 at Manchester City. Diego Simeone is consistently elite (+0.26 at Atlético over 267 games). Conte's Juventus stints are spectacular (+0.44, +0.38). Pochettino climbed from -0.02 at Espanyol to +0.30 at Tottenham. Carlo Ancelotti is the surprise: across his AC Milan, Chelsea, PSG, Real Madrid and Bayern tenures, his averages range from -0.27 to +0.03 — a man with five Champions League trophies on his CV looks, in this metric, like a roughly average coach paired with elite squads.

ana_18.label: Shrinkage in numbers: 461 games of zero must be added
ana_18.content: The Economist's optimisation found that 461 games of league-average performance must be added to any manager's track record to produce the best out-of-sample forecast of his next job. This is a brutal multiplier on early-career evidence. A coach with a single 38-game season retains only 7.6% of his record after shrinkage — meaning even an apparently incandescent debut campaign carries almost no signal. A three-season tenure (114 games) retains 19.8%. Ten seasons (380 games) retains 45.2%. Sir Alex Ferguson's data-covered tenure of 342 games retains 42.6%. Effectively, managers must work two decades before the model lets them speak for themselves.

data_table.description: Career carry-over fraction at various tenure lengths under 461-game shrinkage

ana_12.label: Most over-performing team-seasons (Leicester 2016 leads)
ana_12.content: Leicester City's 2015-16 Premier League title-winning season is the most extreme team-season in the entire dataset, beating its FIFA-rating-based forecast by +1.07 points per game — across 38 games, that is roughly 41 extra league points. RB Leipzig's 2017 Bundesliga campaign is second (+0.92), Liverpool 2019 third (+0.87 ppg). On the underperforming side, Monaco 2019 was the biggest collapse (-0.91 ppg), followed by Chelsea's post-title 2016 season (-0.83). The presence of Dortmund 2015 in the bottom five is sobering: that was Klopp's farewell campaign, and even his Dortmund missed expectations badly that one season.

caveats.content: FIFA player ratings are themselves a noisy estimate of player skill, blending objective stats and ~9,000 subjective scout assessments. The forecast inherits that noise, which is one reason a roughly 7-point-per-team-per-season error band is unavoidable.
Survivorship bias: managers who fail badly are sacked quickly, so very long tenures necessarily belong to coaches who were already over-performing. This biases the sample of long careers upward.

The model attributes residual variance after squad quality entirely to the manager. Other factors (injuries, refereeing luck, off-field instability, owner interference) are folded into the same residual.
